  Readable gloss: "At its core this verb depicts the action of moving living beings from one place to another by urging, guiding, or compelling them forward. Whether a shepherd driving a flock (Exodus 3:1), a king leading a nation (Psalm 80:1), or God guiding His people with deliberate care (Psalm 78:26), the word spans a spectrum from gentle guidance to forceful removal. The Aramaic cognate emphasizes 'leading,' while the Arabic root stresses 'keeping to the road,' together illuminating a verb that encompasses both the tender hand of the shepherd and the harsh compulsion of the captor."

    Enriched: Leading or conducting people on a journey or along a path. Psalm 80:1 invokes God as the one who 'leads Joseph like a flock,' and Ecclesiastes 2:3 uses it for guiding one's own heart. Spanish 'guiaré/conducirá' and French 'conduire' reflect the active, purposeful sense of a leader bringing others along a route, whether physical or figurative.
    Existing Spanish translations: Te-guiaré, conducidos, conducirá, conductor-de, guiando, los-conducirá, y-condujo
  Sense 2: "drive, herd livestock"
    Enriched: The concrete pastoral sense of physically driving or herding livestock -- flocks, herds, or donkeys -- by urging them forward. Genesis 31:18 describes Jacob driving away all his cattle, and 1 Samuel 23:5 tells of David driving off the Philistines' livestock. Spanish 'condujo' and French 'chasse' (drove) capture the energetic, hands-on nature of moving animals en masse.
    Existing Spanish translations: Conduce, Y-condujo, conduce, conduciendo, condujeron, guiaban, llevan;, y-condujo, y-que-conduzcan
  Sense 3: "guide carefully (Piel)"
    Enriched: The Piel intensive stem conveys deliberate, sustained guidance by a figure of authority. God guides the east wind across the sky (Psalm 78:26) and leads His people through the wilderness (Exodus 14:25, where He 'drove' the Egyptian chariot wheels). French 'conduire' and Spanish 'guiaste' (you guided) reflect the careful, authoritative quality that distinguishes this intensified stem from ordinary ...
    Existing Spanish translations: conducirá, e-hizo-conducirlos, guiaste, los-guiará, nos-guiará, te-llevará, y-guió, y-los-guió
  Sense 4: "drive away, carry off"
    Enriched: Driving away by force or carrying off as plunder. Genesis 31:26 has Laban accusing Jacob of 'driving away my daughters like captives,' and 1 Samuel 30:2 describes the Amalekites driving off captives. Lamentations 3:2 extends this to God driving the speaker into darkness. Spanish 'condujeron' and the shift toward compulsion mark this sense as the harsh, hostile end of the verb's semantic range.
    Existing Spanish translations: condujo, me-ha-guiado, y-condujeron, y-condujiste
